cards.title: Polynomial exact metric sparsifiers with a crossing-edge budget
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,c>0 such that the following holds? For every finite simple undirected unweighted graph G=(V,E), terminal set T⊆V of size r, and integer p≥0, there is a set Z⊆E with |Z|≤C(1+p+r)^c having this universal property: for every finite nonempty label set D, every metric μ:D×D→R_{≥0}, and every terminal labeling τ:T→D, if there exists a labeling λ:V→D extending τ with at most p crossing edges, then some labeling λ* of minimum μ-cost among all such budget-feasible extensions has all its crossing edges in Z. The same Z must work simultaneously for every D,μ,τ and depends only on G,T,p. This is the polynomial-size version of the contraction-based metric-sparsifier property in the source’s Theorem 22; that theorem’s earlier quasipolynomial upper-bound claim was later retracted.
cards.why: Would determine whether a graph can be compressed once for every metric-labeling objective under a bounded number of label changes, a stronger form of reusable exact information than preserving ordinary terminal cut values.
cards.status_note: Recovered the exact universal-set property from conference Theorem 22 and read the corrected full version’s explicit retraction and retained question. Checked the journal metadata and indexed author-manuscript retraction, the 2024 multicut theorem and later sparsifier searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution of this exact metric/budget property was found; the retracted theorem is not treated as established progress.

sentences: A graph with terminals is queried by choosing labels for the terminals and a metric on the labels.
The goal is a small retained edge set that supports an optimal extension for every such query.
Only labelings with at most p crossing edges are compared, and the retained set must have size polynomial in p plus the number of terminals.
The original claimed quasipolynomial metric-sparsifier result was explicitly retracted in the corrected paper.
Ordinary multicut sparsifiers preserve a different collection of values and do not settle this universal metric question.

cards.definitions: A crossing edge of λ is an edge uv with λ(u)≠λ(v). Write X(λ)={uv∈E:λ(u)≠λ(v)} and cost_μ(λ)=Σ_{uv∈E}μ(λ(u),λ(v)). A metric has μ(a,b)=μ(b,a), μ(a,b)=0 exactly when a=b, and μ(a,c)≤μ(a,b)+μ(b,c). The admissible labelings for a query are B(G,T,p,D,τ)={λ:V→D:λ|_T=τ and |X(λ)|≤p}. If B is nonempty, the finite set D^V ensures that min_{λ∈B}cost_μ(λ) is attained. The universal requirement is that this minimum equals the minimum with the additional constraint X(λ)⊆Z; in particular the latter feasible set must be nonempty. The number p bounds crossings, not the real-valued metric cost. Labeling τ need not be injective or surjective, and |D| is unbounded independently of p+r. The constants C,c may not depend on the graph, budget, label set, metric or terminal labeling. Using 1+p+r only handles zero parameters and is asymptotically equivalent to polynomial size in p+r. Restricting all edges outside Z to have equal endpoint labels is exactly the labeling constraint imposed by contracting those edges; Z measures the original retained edges. The question is existence of this universal set, not the running time to find it, so it neither assumes rational metric entries nor a numerical oracle for them. Exact equality of optimum values is required; no multiplicative or additive error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal polynomial bound, or refute it by showing that no fixed constants C,c can bound the required retained edges over all G,T,p. A negative result must respect the quantifier order: every candidate small Z must fail for some label set, metric and terminal labeling with a feasible budgeted extension. Hardness of finding a small Z does not disprove its existence. Bounds for one fixed metric, a fixed number of labels, ordinary terminal cut values, or approximate values do not settle this target.

context_blocks.title: One graph must support every metric query
context_blocks.text: A 0-Extension instance extends fixed labels on terminals to the rest of a graph while minimizing metric distances across edges. The desired sparsifier is chosen before either the metric or the terminal labels, and must retain an optimal extension whenever the crossing-edge budget is feasible.

context_blocks.title: The source’s parameter is not just the terminal count
context_blocks.text: Theorem 22 uses p+r, with p counting disagreeing endpoints and r counting terminals. This differs from the total terminal degree used for ordinary multicut-mimicking networks elsewhere in the paper. An unrestricted terminal-count lower bound is therefore not automatically a lower bound for this question.

context_blocks.title: The earlier quasipolynomial claim was retracted
context_blocks.text: The corrected March 2021 version explicitly reports an incorrect proof for the preliminary 0-Extension claims and retracts the claimed quasipolynomial metric sparsifiers. It retains the underlying existence question. The retraction also appears in the accepted journal manuscript; the paper’s ordinary multicut results and the earlier Reidl–Wahlström results are stated to be unaffected.

context_blocks.title: Later cut sparsifiers preserve a different family of quantities
context_blocks.text: Anand, Lee, Li and Saranurak’s 2024 work obtains randomized polynomial-time ordinary multicut-mimicking networks with k^{O(log² k)} size, where k is total terminal degree. Their preserved quantities are minimum multiway-cut cardinalities for terminal partitions. This does not reestablish the retracted all-metrics, crossing-budget property.

cards.context:
A 0-Extension instance extends fixed labels on terminals to the rest of a graph while minimizing metric distances across edges. The desired sparsifier is chosen before either the metric or the terminal labels, and must retain an optimal extension whenever the crossing-edge budget is feasible.

Theorem 22 uses p+r, with p counting disagreeing endpoints and r counting terminals. This differs from the total terminal degree used for ordinary multicut-mimicking networks elsewhere in the paper. An unrestricted terminal-count lower bound is therefore not automatically a lower bound for this question.

The corrected March 2021 version explicitly reports an incorrect proof for the preliminary 0-Extension claims and retracts the claimed quasipolynomial metric sparsifiers. It retains the underlying existence question. The retraction also appears in the accepted journal manuscript; the paper’s ordinary multicut results and the earlier Reidl–Wahlström results are stated to be unaffected.

Anand, Lee, Li and Saranurak’s 2024 work obtains randomized polynomial-time ordinary multicut-mimicking networks with k^{O(log² k)} size, where k is total terminal degree. Their preserved quantities are minimum multiway-cut cardinalities for terminal partitions. This does not reestablish the retracted all-metrics, crossing-budget property.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
